name: Gecko
description: Billions of nanoscale setae generate van der Waals adhesion supporting full body weight on glass. Self-cleaning: contaminants bind to surfaces more than setae, ejecting dirt per step. Directional adhesion activates with shear angle, releases with peel.

core_attributes.neurology: proprioceptive toe-pad feedback, rapid detachment motor circuits
core_attributes.pattern: van der Waals nanoscale adhesion, self-cleaning surfaces, directional grip geometry

scope.definition: Shear adhesion force per unit area of Tokay gecko toe pad relative to body weight — expressed as body-weight multiples the adhesion can support in controlled shear pull tests.

evidence.source: Autumn et al. (2000) 'Adhesive force of a single gecko foot-hair', Nature 405:681-685; Autumn et al. (2002) 'Evidence for van der Waals adhesion in gecko setae', PNAS 99:12252-12256.
cross_domain_examples: single gecko seta produces 200 µN shear force — 10× body-weight equivalent per seta area
van der Waals forces confirmed as mechanism — adhesion works in vacuum, eliminates suction/glue hypotheses
gecko-inspired dry adhesive tapes achieve 0.80 of natural adhesion force in prototype testing
spider attachment pads: convergent hierarchical microstructure adhesion system achieving similar shear forces

scope.falsifiability: If gecko adhesion is measured to be temperature-independent and humidity-independent in full shear-force conditions, van der Waals electrostatic mechanism (vs capillary) is confirmed.
scope.measurement_limits: Adhesion strength is direction-dependent — shear outperforms peel by 10:1. Contamination reduces adhesion by 60-80%. Gecko setae self-clean via repeated contact cycles — critical for maintained function.

scope.definition: Fraction of contaminating particles (20-µm glass spheres) removed from gecko toe pad per step on clean glass — measured by particle count before and after controlled locomotion.

evidence.source: Hansen & Autumn (2005) 'Evidence for self-cleaning in gecko setae', PNAS 102:385-389.
cross_domain_examples: 90.5% of glass microspheres shed from gecko toe pad within first 4 steps on clean glass
particle adhesion to substrate preferred over seta adhesion — equilibrium thermodynamics drives self-cleaning
lotus leaf self-cleaning: superhydrophobic micro-papillae cause water droplets to roll off carrying particles — analogous structural self-cleaning principle

scope.falsifiability: If particle removal rate from contaminated setae does not exceed 80% in 4 steps on clean substrates, the self-cleaning mechanism fails to explain sustained gecko adhesion.
scope.measurement_limits: Self-cleaning efficiency decreases with particle size (>50 µm particles not shed efficiently) and with oily contaminants (chemical affinity overrides mechanical cleaning). Only validated for dry environments.

scope.definition: Ratio of shear adhesion force in optimal toe-curl direction to anti-optimal direction (setae angled backward vs forward) — demonstrating directional asymmetry of hierarchical setal system.

evidence.source: Autumn et al. (2006) 'Dynamics of geckos running on inclines', Journal of Experimental Biology 209:3014-3021; Gravish et al. (2010) 'Rate-dependent frictional adhesion in natural and synthetic gecko setae'.
cross_domain_examples: setal shear force ratio (optimal/anti-optimal) = 4-6:1 — strongly direction-coded adhesion
gecko releases from surface by toe hyperextension — same angle-dependent mechanism for detachment
directional adhesive composites for robotic climbing: bio-inspired dry adhesives with 3:1 directionality

scope.falsifiability: If measured shear force in anti-optimal setal orientation exceeds 50% of optimal orientation, the directional adhesion model does not explain preferential toe-curl attachment strategy.
scope.measurement_limits: Directionality is substrate-roughness dependent — works best on smooth surfaces. On rough surfaces (Ra > 10 µm) directionality decreases as setae cannot fully contact substrate.
